title: Computing the Internet Checksum
summary: Summarizes techniques and algorithms for efficiently computing the Internet checksum. It is not a standard but a collection of useful implementation tricks. It was updated by RFC 1141.

eli5.summary: The checksum is a quick math check that tells if a packet got scrambled. This memo shares clever ways to do the math fast.

questions: how to compute the internet checksum
how to calculate the ip checksum quickly
how to compute the internet checksum quickly
how to update a checksum incrementally
subtitle: A collection of tricks for computing the Internet checksum quickly, with worked examples and code for several CPUs.

tldr.problem: The checksum used by IP, UDP and TCP must be computed for every packet, and on fast networks it can become one of the limits on TCP performance.
tldr.mechanism: The memo restates the 16-bit one's complement sum, lists its mathematical properties, and shows how to exploit them with wider words, deferred carries, unrolled loops and incremental updates.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 1141.

today: RFC 1071 is Informational, not a standard, and it was updated by RFC 1141. It does not define the checksum field of any protocol; it collects implementation techniques.

sections.title: The Internet Checksum in Outline
sections.content:
This memo is about computing the checksum used by IP, UDP and TCP efficiently. Its argument is that a fast checksum matters: a fraction of a microsecond per TCP data byte adds up to a significant CPU saving, so it is usually appropriate to hand-craft the routine.

The algorithm is simple. Adjacent octets are paired into 16-bit integers and their one's complement sum is formed. To generate a checksum, the checksum field is cleared, the sum is computed over the octets concerned, and the one's complement of that sum goes in the field. To check one, the sum is computed again including the checksum field, and the check succeeds if the result is all 1 bits. If the byte count is odd, the last byte is paired with a zero.

On a two's complement machine the one's complement sum needs an end-around carry: any overflow out of the top bit is added back into the bottom bit.
sections.eli5: You add up all the numbers in the message and write down a special check number. The receiver adds everything again, check number included, and if the answer comes out right, nothing got scrambled.

sections.title: Properties That Make It Fast
sections.content:
Section 2 lists mathematical properties of the sum that an implementer can use.

  • Commutative and associative. The sum can be done in any order and split into groups, as long as the even and odd byte positions are respected.
  • Byte order independence. Summing in either byte order gives the same result with the bytes swapped, so little-endian and big-endian machines can use the same code.
  • Parallel summation. On machines with wider words, such as 32 bits, several bytes can be added at once and the long sum is then folded into 16 bits, adding any new end-around carries.

Four coding techniques are added: deferred carries (accumulate in a 32-bit register and add the carries at the end), unwinding loops, combining the checksum with data copying so memory is read once, and incremental update.
sections.eli5: Adding is forgiving. You can add the numbers in any order or in chunks, and you get the same answer. That lets a computer add several at a time.

sections.title: Incremental Update and Worked Examples
sections.content:
If one header field changes, the whole checksum need not be recomputed. The best-known example is a gateway changing the TTL field in the IP header. The RFC's rule is to add the difference of the changed 16-bit integers: given the old value m, the new value m' and the old checksum C, the new checksum is C' = C + (m' - m).

Section 3 then works through numeric examples in hex. The same eight bytes are summed byte by byte, as 16-bit words in normal and swapped order, and 32 bits at a time in three orders. Every route reaches the same final result, ddf2. A last example splits the data into two groups, with the second starting on an odd boundary.
sections.eli5: If only one number in a long list changes, you do not add the whole list again. You just fix the total by the amount that changed.

sections.title: Code for Different CPUs
sections.content:
Section 4 gives the core of the algorithm, without surrounding code, for several processors. A C version sums 16 bits at a time into a 32-bit accumulator, adds a left-over byte if there is one, folds the sum to 16 bits and complements it.

The other examples are assembler. A Motorola 68020 routine by Van Jacobson sums 32 bits at a time with the loop unrolled 16 times, and was measured at 134 usec/kB on random data with a 20MHz clock. A Cray routine by Charley Kline uses vector operations on blocks of up to 512 bytes. An IBM 370 routine sums four bytes at a time and was timed on an IBM 3090 at 27 usec/KB when summing all one bits.
sections.eli5: The memo shows the same trick written out for several different kinds of computers, like one recipe cooked in several different kitchens.

sections.title: Appendix: Plummer's IEN 45
sections.content:
The checksum's properties were first discussed by Bill Plummer in IEN 45, "TCP Checksum Function Design" (5 June 1978). Because that note was not widely available, the memo reproduces it as an extended appendix.

IEN 45 lists what a TCP checksum should keep: it is commutative, has an identity and an inverse, is associative, is fast on varied machines, is systematic (the data bytes are unchanged, so gateways can read fields like the destination address), and can be modified incrementally. One's complement addition beats two's complement because it is equally sensitive to errors in every bit position, and it beats exclusive-OR, which permits an even number of drops in a bit channel.

The note also weighs alternatives, including a "product code" and CRC schemes, and concludes that the product code is viable but needs gateways to decode messages at least partly. It is also wary of checking checksums in a front-end machine, since that would destroy the end-to-end character of the checksum.
sections.eli5: An old note explains why simple adding was a smart choice for catching mistakes. It is easy to do, easy to fix up, and does not change the message itself.

viz.caption: WHY THE SUM IS EASY TO SPEED UP

items.title: Any order
items.text: Commutative and associative, so the sum can be split into groups.

items.title: Either byte order
items.text: Little-endian and big-endian machines get the same result, bytes swapped.

items.title: Wide words
items.text: Add 32 bits at a time, then fold into 16 bits.

items.title: Incremental
items.text: Add the difference when one field changes.
